sources.description: lib/learning-paths (FDE, DSA Foundations), gated by env switches
Supabase override table (admin edits, custom questions, hides). Not readable from the repository.
lib/quiz-data.ts coreQuestions outside code-snippets: module-private, exported nowhere

items.objective: Define artificial intelligence as a field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, not a single program or a robot.
defects: hint 'Let's start with the big picture.' is filler: it is not written for this question or this misconception
'Any computer connected to the internet' is a joke option no learner weighs
the key is the longest option by a wide margin, which is a length cue
items.rationale: The key and explanation are sound literacy for level 1; the hint is filler and one distractor is a joke. A hint and option pass fixes both without changing the objective.
evidence: knowledge: AI is standardly defined as the field of building systems that perform tasks requiring human intelligence

cs.notes: Reviewer marked the Czech verified, but the audit rewrote options and explanation, so all four fields are new.

problems: hint restates the key: 'Ask which option describes a field rather than a device' points straight at the only option that begins 'The field of'
evidence: knowledge: AI is standardly defined as the field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence
verification.notes: Key, options and explanation are sound; only the hint hands over the answer.

items.objective: State what a supervised training set contains: inputs paired with their correct outputs.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a tag echo
'Random noise with no structure' is a joke option
explanation restates the key and never says why the reward option is a different paradigm
items.rationale: Core vocabulary with a correct key; the hint is boilerplate and one distractor is unserious. Replacing it with self-supervision also sets up the pretraining levels later in this topic.
evidence: knowledge: supervised learning requires labeled input-output pairs
fetched: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/glossary - pretraining predicts the next word from preceding context (self-supervised)
fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/glossary: pretraining runs on 'a large unlabeled corpus of text' with models 'pretrained to predict the next word, given the previous context'
verification.notes: The hint's 'tell the model it was wrong' fits the reward option too, so it does not resolve the item; the self-supervised distractor is correctly separated from supervised in the explanation.

items.objective: Recognize the case for fine-tuning: stable behavior, style or format, as opposed to which facts reach the model.
defects: three distractors ('latest news', 'facts change every hour', 'avoid any training cost') are all the freshness case restated, so the item is answerable by elimination
the key is markedly longer than the distractors
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on prompting' tag appended
explanation does not note that output shape is now often enforced with a response schema rather than a fine-tune
items.rationale: The complement to rm-ai-99 and worth keeping, but three interchangeable freshness distractors let a learner answer without knowing the fine-tuning case. Making each distractor a distinct retrieval job is what turns the elimination into a real judgment.
evidence: knowledge: fine-tuning changes behavior encoded in weights; retrieval changes which facts appear in the context

problems: hint asks which option is about behavior rather than which facts reach the model, which is the explanation's discriminator and selects the only behavior option
evidence: knowledge: fine-tuning changes behavior encoded in weights; freshness, citation and post-cutoff facts are retrieval's job
verification.notes: Response-schema note in the explanation is a fair present-day caveat for the format case.

items.objective: Place embeddings in a RAG pipeline: chunks and query become vectors so nearest-neighbor search can find passages by meaning.
items.retireReason: second reading: duplicate of rm-ai-78 in this batch: both ask what embeddings do in a RAG pipeline and both key the same proposition (embed chunks and query, retrieve by similarity); the first reviewer's own note on rm-ai-78 designates that item as the survivor
defects: all three distractors ('set the temperature', 'translate the answer', 'compress the model weights') are unrelated to retrieval
the key is markedly longer than the distractors
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on embeddings' tag appended
items.rationale: The item that connects the embeddings level to the RAG level, correctly keyed and clearly explained. Replacing three unrelated options with real pipeline stages - summarization, reranking, compression - is what makes the choice discriminating.
evidence: knowledge: RAG retrieval embeds chunks at index time and the query per request, then runs nearest-neighbor search

cs.notes: Czech asks the same question with the same options in the same order and an equivalent explanation. Rewritten options, hint and explanation need new Czech.

problems: duplicate of rm-ai-78 in this batch: both ask what embeddings do in a RAG pipeline and both key the same proposition (embed chunks and query, retrieve by similarity); the first reviewer's own note on rm-ai-78 designates that item as the survivor
evidence: node v22.22.2: cos([1,0,1],[1,1,0]) = 0.5 and cos([1,2,3],[2,4,6]) = 1, so the two figures quoted in this explanation are right
knowledge: RAG embeds chunks at index time and the query per request, then runs nearest-neighbor search
verification.notes: The content is sound and the pipeline-stage distractors are better than rm-ai-78's, so if a later pass prefers to retire rm-ai-78 instead, this item can be restored unchanged apart from its hint, which is 26 words and hands over the word vectors.

items.objective: Define grounding as tying an answer to source material supplied to the model.
items.retireReason: term-definition duplicate of rm-ai-94 and rm-ai-97
defects: pure vocabulary recall for a term rm-ai-94 already exercises in a decision and rm-ai-97 already describes as a mechanism
'Lowering the temperature to zero', 'Limiting the response length' and 'Running the model offline' are filler, leaving the key as the only content-bearing option
hint is the generic shape-based fallback, and its 'Focus on RAG' tag points at the neighboring concept rather than this one
explanation restates the key
items.rationale: The level already spends rm-ai-94 on choosing grounding and rm-ai-97 on how retrieval performs it, so this item adds only the word. The one idea that would make it distinct - that a grounded answer can still misread its source - is where rm-ai-94's rewritten explanation ends.
evidence: run: within this batch, rm-ai-94 keys 'provide the relevant source text in the prompt so the model can ground its answer' and rm-ai-97 keys the retrieve-then-prompt mechanism; this item keys the same idea as a definition

cs.notes: Czech is a faithful parallel translation of the question, options and explanation. No new Czech needed if the item is retired.

items.objective: State the freshness limitation of fine-tuning: its knowledge is fixed at training time and needs a retrain to update.
items.retireReason: third statement of the freshness contrast already taught by rm-ai-99 and rm-ai-100
defects: the freshness contrast is the whole content of rm-ai-99 and the discriminating axis of rm-ai-100; this item asks it a third time with no new decision attached
explanation repeats rm-ai-99's explanation almost verbatim ('you update the document store, not the model' versus 'RAG refreshes information by updating the retrievable corpus')
'automatically learns tomorrow's facts', 'cannot change model behavior at all' and 'removes the need for any data' are three absurd options
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on RAG' tag appended
items.rationale: Correct but redundant: rm-ai-99 makes the same point inside a real architecture choice and rm-ai-100 uses it as the discriminator, so a third abstract restatement teaches nothing more. Its option set is also the weakest of the three.
evidence: run: within this batch, rm-ai-99 keys 'use RAG to retrieve the latest relevant documents at query time' and rm-ai-100 keys the style-versus-freshness split; this item restates the same contrast

cs.notes: Czech mirrors the English question, options and explanation in order. No new Czech needed if the item is retired.

items.objective: Split responsibilities between the layers: stable behavior in the prompt or weights, changing facts in retrieval.
defects: 'Combine approaches' against two 'only X, never Y' mirror options and a joke is the classic giveaway shape
'Increase top-p and hope for the best' is filler
capitalized AND in the stem is test-taking emphasis
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on fine-tuning' tag appended
items.rationale: The corrective to the false dilemma the level sets up is worth an item, but 'combine both' against three absolutes is answerable on shape alone. Asking which split of responsibilities to adopt keeps the objective and forces the learner to match each requirement to a layer.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing - input tokens are billed per request, so a corpus-sized system prompt is paid for on every call
fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing : input tokens are billed per request per million, so a corpus-sized system prompt is paid for on every call
verification.notes: Hint states the framing (one requirement changes weekly, one does not) without saying which layer absorbs which, and the weekly-fine-tune option is still a live temptation under it.

items.objective: Explain what a message role expresses in a chat API: the source of the message, which sets how much authority its instructions carry.
defects: the key and the explanation both name 'system, user, and assistant' as the typical roles, which is stale at both major vendors: Anthropic's Messages API states there is no system role for input messages and takes instructions in a top-level system parameter, and OpenAI's current text-generation guidance documents developer, user and assistant with no system role
the explanation gives the stale role list a second time as fact, so the item teaches a name a learner will not find in either provider's current API
'Pricing tiers', 'Token compression methods' and 'The model's temperature levels' are filler
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on messages' tag appended
the key never says what the role is for - instruction precedence - which is the reason the field exists
items.rationale: The concept is right and the key is still the only defensible option, but the role names inside it are out of date at both vendors a learner would call, which is exactly the claim that must be checked against current docs. Rewriting the key around instruction precedence keeps the objective and makes the vendor-specific names an explicitly dated detail in the explanation.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages - 'you can use the top-level system parameter - there is no "system" role for input messages in the Messages API'

https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/text - documents developer ('instructions provided by the application developer, prioritized ahead of user messages'), user and assistant; no system role appears

problems: hint says two messages with identical text can carry different weight, which is the key's authority clause stated before the options are read
evidence: fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages : there is no system role for input messages in the Messages API; the system prompt is a top-level system parameter
fetched https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/text : roles are developer (instructions from the application developer, prioritized ahead of user messages), user and assistant
verification.notes: The dated system-user-assistant claim flagged in the first pass is fixed: the key no longer names roles and the explanation gives each vendor's current shape, both of which match the docs I fetched today.

items.objective: Know how pay-per-use model APIs meter cost: input and output tokens, priced separately.
defects: the key is markedly longer and the only detailed option
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on pricing' tag appended

explanation stops at 'separate rates for input and output' and omits that current pricing splits input further into base, cache-write and cache-read rates, which is where most of the cost control actually lives
neither key nor explanation says that output is the expensive side, which is the fact that changes how you write a prompt
items.rationale: Correct and among the most consequential facts in the level, since cost is the constraint that shapes prompt design. The rewrite keeps every claim undated - shape, not figures - while adding the output-costs-more asymmetry and the cache-rate split that current pricing pages document.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing - per-model table has separate 'Base input tokens', '5m cache writes', '1h cache writes', 'Cache hits and refreshes' and 'Output tokens' columns, all priced per million tokens, with output several times base input
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing - 'Cache read (hit) 0.1x base input price'; Batch API gives 'a 50% discount on both input and output tokens'

problems: hint asks whether the meter can tell two quantities apart, which is the metered-separately half of the key
evidence: fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing : the per-model table prices Base input tokens, 5m cache writes, 1h cache writes, Cache hits and refreshes and Output tokens per MTok, with output five times base input on every current model
verification.notes: Every claim in the explanation, including the cache-rate split of input, checks out against the current pricing table, and none of it is stated as a figure that will date.

items.objective: Explain what streaming changes: tokens are delivered as produced, improving perceived rather than total latency.
defects: 'It encrypts the response' and 'It reduces the total token cost to zero' are absurd; 'It guarantees deterministic output' is unrelated to the question
the key is markedly longer than the distractors
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on streaming' tag appended
explanation does not state the point learners actually get wrong: total generation time and total cost are unchanged
items.rationale: Correct but built on three throwaway options, and it never names the misconception worth correcting - that streaming makes generation faster. Putting that belief in as the strongest distractor is what makes the item worth asking.
evidence: knowledge: streaming changes delivery of already-generated tokens; it does not change decode speed or token accounting

problems: hint offers the binary the key resolves (how fast it is produced, or when the client can show it), so the learner never has to weigh the faster-overall distractor
evidence: knowledge: streaming changes delivery of tokens as they are generated; decode speed, total generation time and token accounting are unchanged
verification.notes: Explanation correctly separates perceived from total latency and names the client-side cost, which is the honest trade.

items.objective: Read HTTP 429 from a model API as a rate or spend limit and respond with the documented retry behavior.
defects: 'The model hallucinated', 'The API key is correct' and 'Streaming finished successfully' are not answers to the question, let alone misconceptions
the key is markedly longer than the distractors
hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a 'Focus on rate-limits' tag appended

the explanation's remedy list ('backoff, retries, and request batching') omits the retry-after header, which is the documented instruction, and retrying without honoring it is what turns a 429 into a retry storm
it does not mention that a 429 can also mean a spend cap has been reached, in which case retrying keeps failing until the limit is raised
items.rationale: The key is right and the skill is genuinely operational, but three options that do not answer the question make it free, and the remedy given is the one that causes retry storms. Turning the distractors into the neighboring status codes teaches the whole 4xx/5xx neighborhood at no extra cost.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits - 'If you exceed any of the rate limits you will get a 429 error describing which rate limit was exceeded, along with a retry-after header indicating how long to wait'

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits - at the spend cap 'API requests return HTTP 429' and 'the response has no retry-after header. Retrying, including the SDKs' automatic retries, fails until access resumes'

problems: hint says 429 is the client doing too much of something, which is the key in other words
evidence: fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits : exceeding a rate limit returns a 429 describing which limit was exceeded, with a retry-after header indicating how long to wait

fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits : at the spend cap requests return HTTP 429 with no retry-after header, and retrying, including the SDKs' automatic retries, fails until access resumes
verification.notes: Both documented claims in the explanation check out, and the neighboring status codes make the distractors teach rather than pad.

items.objective: Separate standing instructions (system) from the current request (user) in a chat API call.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback

stem assumes every chat API exposes a system message role; Anthropic's Messages API has no system role for input messages and takes a top-level system parameter, and OpenAI's Responses API uses a developer role
explanation restates the key and never addresses the reversed-roles distractor or the token-cost distractor
items.rationale: The key is the only defensible answer and the objective is central to calling any model API, but the stem keys a message shape one major vendor no longer has and the hint is filler. Naming both shapes keeps the item accurate as APIs move.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages - "there is no \"system\" role for input messages in the Messages API"; system is a top-level parameter
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/api-reference/chat/create - ChatCompletionDeveloperMessageParam: "With o1 models and newer, developer messages replace the previous system messages"
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages - "there is no \"system\" role for input messages in the Messages API"; top-level `system` parameter
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/api-reference/chat/create - "With o1 models and newer, `developer` messages replace the previous `system` messages"
knowledge: the stem now says 'system instructions' and hedges with 'In most chat model APIs', so it no longer keys a role Anthropic does not expose
verification.notes: Rewrite drops the stale 'system message' role framing and the explanation names both vendor shapes, both of which I confirmed against the primary docs.

items.objective: Recognize clustering unlabeled data as unsupervised learning.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a tag echo
explanation names clustering but does not say what disqualifies the two labeled tasks
items.rationale: Well-built item: four options that map cleanly onto the three paradigms, correct key, on-level. Only the filler hint and the thin explanation need work.
evidence: knowledge: clustering is the canonical unsupervised task; regression and classification on labeled data are supervised

cs.notes: 'Temperature' here is weather temperature, so it is 'teplota'; the sampling parameter keeps the English name elsewhere.

evidence: knowledge: clustering unlabeled data is the canonical unsupervised task; regression and classification on labeled data are supervised
verification.notes: The hint's no-labels criterion also fits the reinforcement-learning option, so it narrows without resolving.

items.objective: Handle a 429 from a model API with exponential backoff and the Retry-After header.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
distractor 'Switch to temperature 0' is unrelated to rate limiting rather than a misconception about it
explanation never says why a fixed or immediate retry fails
items.rationale: Correct, current and directly operational; only the filler hint, one off-topic distractor and a thin explanation hold it back. The retry rule transfers to every rate-limited API, not just model endpoints.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits - "you will get a 429 error describing which rate limit was exceeded, along with a retry-after header indicating how long to wait"; "Earlier retries will fail"
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits - "429 error describing which rate limit was exceeded, along with a retry-after header indicating how long to wait"; "Earlier retries will fail"
knowledge: jitter decorrelates retries across clients; a fixed 100 ms retry and parallel fan-out both keep the per-minute budget saturated
verification.notes: Key and both quoted retry-after claims verified; the word 'robust' in the stem is pre-existing and untouched by the rewrite, so I left it rather than desyncing the stem.

items.objective: Explain why token counts, not characters or words, govern context limits and cost.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
option 3 ('Token counts never affect cost') is the direct negation of the key, which flags the key by pairing
options 0 and 1 are not misconceptions anyone holds
explanation restates the key without correcting any wrong belief
items.rationale: The objective is sound and the key is correct, but three of four options are throwaways and one is the key's negation. Replacing them with real tokenizer misconceptions makes the item test what it claims to.
evidence: knowledge: providers meter both context length and billing in tokens; BPE-style tokenizers give no fixed character-per-token ratio

problems: hint paraphrases the key: 'which unit the provider's limit and the provider's invoice are both written in' is the key's 'context windows and pricing are both measured in tokens'
evidence: knowledge: BPE-style tokenizers give no fixed characters-per-token ratio, and providers meter both context length and billing in tokens
knowledge: a learner reading the old hint could pick option 2 without knowing anything, since it is the only option naming both the limit and the price
verification.notes: New hint points at the two tokenizer misconceptions in options 0 and 1 instead of restating the key.

items.objective: Choose the sound mitigation when a request would exceed the context window.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
correct option is markedly longer and more detailed than the three distractors
two distractors (raise temperature, send twice) are not mistakes anyone makes about context limits
explanation restates the key
items.rationale: A real operational decision with a correct key, spoiled by a conspicuously detailed correct option and joke distractors. The max_tokens distractor turns it into a test of how the budget is actually split.
evidence: knowledge: the context window bounds input plus generated output for a single request; max_tokens reserves part of that same budget

problems: the reviewer's own defect list called 'send the request twice' a non-mistake and the rewrite kept it
hint asserted the tested premise ('the limit counts the prompt and the reply together'), which is the clause that makes the max_tokens distractor wrong
evidence: knowledge: the context window bounds input plus generated output for one request; max_tokens reserves part of that same budget
knowledge: streaming is a transport concern and changes neither the token count nor the window check
verification.notes: Replaced the leftover joke distractor with the streaming misconception, kept the key at index 1, and rewrote the hint so it no longer hands over the shared-budget rule.

items.objective: State the purpose of a system prompt in a chat assistant.
items.retireReason: duplicates rm-ai-109, which teaches the same system/user split and has a real misconception as a distractor
defects: teaches nothing beyond rm-ai-109, one level earlier in the same topic
two distractors (storing the user's password, setting GPU clock speed) are jokes, so the key is identifiable without knowing anything
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation restates the key
items.rationale: The objective is already covered by rm-ai-109, which contrasts system with user instructions instead of defining one of them alone. What remains here is a definition surrounded by jokes.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages - system prompt is supplied through the top-level system parameter, confirming the same concept tested by rm-ai-109

cs.notes: Faithful parallel translation of question, options and explanation.

items.objective: Explain that a stateless chat API only sees prior turns because the client resends them.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
distractor 'guesses based on the user's name' is nonsense rather than a misconception
explanation does not mention that some APIs now offer opt-in server-side threading, which is where a learner will meet the exception
items.rationale: This is the single most useful mental model in the level and the key is right, but the distractors miss the belief learners actually hold - that the model remembers. The weights distractor and the threading caveat both address that.
evidence: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state - manual history management is supported alongside previous_response_id and the Conversations API for server-side state

problems: hint's second sentence ('what has to be inside the second one for turn one to exist') is the key: the client resends the prior messages
evidence: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state - manual history management alongside previous_response_id and the Conversations API
knowledge: model weights are frozen after training and hold nothing about a given conversation
verification.notes: Explanation's server-side-threading caveat checks out against OpenAI's conversation-state guide; only the hint needed fixing.

items.objective: Predict what breaks as chat history grows and name the usual mitigation.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
stem asks two questions at once without stating that the history is resent each turn
overlaps rm-ai-112's mitigation without adding the cost consequence
explanation restates the key
items.rationale: Worth keeping because it is the consequence of rm-ai-114, but as written it repeats rm-ai-112's mitigation and hides the premise that history is resent. Stating the premise and naming the cost growth makes it a distinct lesson.
evidence: knowledge: stateless chat APIs bill resent history as input tokens on every turn, so both cost and prompt length grow with conversation length

problems: 'The API raises the temperature automatically to fit more in' is a joke distractor the rewrite reworded rather than replaced
key was 117 chars against a 71-char longest distractor (1.65x), so it was pickable by length
hint named both halves of the key (what grows without bound, what it runs into)
evidence: knowledge: temperature is a caller-supplied parameter; no chat API adjusts it on its own
knowledge: streaming changes delivery timing only, so it does not address prompt growth or the window check
verification.notes: Swapped the temperature joke for the latency misconception, trimmed the key to 95 chars, and replaced the hint and matching explanation clause.

items.objective: Know that system-level rules are meant to outrank a conflicting user instruction, and that this is a trained priority rather than an enforced boundary.
defects: explanation states instruction priority as settled ('are meant to take precedence') without saying that it is a trained tendency jailbreaks and injected text routinely defeat
two distractors (the assistant crashes, switches to a random topic) are jokes
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
items.rationale: The intended behavior in the key is right, but the item presents prompt-level precedence as reliable, which is exactly the belief that produces apps with no enforcement outside the prompt. The recency distractor and the added caveat fix both problems.
evidence: knowledge: provider instruction hierarchies rank system above user messages as trained behavior; jailbreak and prompt-injection results show it is not an enforcement boundary

problems: hint states the tested rule ('which instruction the provider trains the model to weigh more heavily'), so the key is pickable from the hint alone
evidence: knowledge: provider instruction hierarchies rank system-level rules above user turns as trained behavior, not as an enforced boundary
knowledge: jailbreak and prompt-injection results show prompt-level precedence is defeatable, which the rewritten explanation now says
verification.notes: The rewrite does fix the flagged 'stated as settled' defect - the explanation now calls the priority a learned tendency and says anything that must not happen needs a check outside the prompt - so only the hint is amended.

items.objective: Define guardrails as constraints spanning safety training, system instructions and application-side checks.
defects: all three distractors (cooling fins, a type of embedding, the token limit) are nonsense, so the item tests nothing
correct option is markedly longer than the distractors
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
as a bare definition it adds little to rm-ai-116, rm-ai-119 and rm-ai-134, which use the concept
items.rationale: As written this is a vocabulary item whose distractors give it away, and it barely clears redundancy with three siblings. Turning the options into the layers guardrails actually live in gives it content the other items do not carry.
evidence: knowledge: production assistants combine model-level safety training, system-prompt rules and application-side filtering; none of the three is sufficient alone

cs.notes: 'guardrails' settled as „mantinely“, glossed once with the English term in this defining question; 'temperature' kept in English per the batch 1 translator.

problems: hint ('the term covers more than one layer... who besides the model provider can add a constraint') selects the only multi-layer option
explanation answered two distractors but never said why a banned-word list compiled into the weights is wrong
evidence: knowledge: safety behavior is learned during training rather than stored as a word list in the parameters
knowledge: production assistants combine model-level training, system-prompt rules and application-side checks
verification.notes: Item sits at the quality floor (3) but clears both gates; hint and the missing distractor rebuttal are the only fixes needed.

items.objective: Pick the mechanism that most reliably enforces a required output format.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
'most directly' plus a compound and/or key makes the correct option both longest and unfalsifiable
the three distractors are not format techniques at all, so no real comparison is made
explanation does not separate best-effort prompting from schema-constrained decoding
items.rationale: The objective is a genuine engineering decision, but the original compares one bundled correct answer against three non-answers. Making all four real format tactics forces the distinction between asking and constraining.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs - "Structured outputs constrain Claude's responses to follow a specific schema"; generally available, beta headers no longer required

https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs - "ensures the model will always generate responses that adhere to your supplied JSON Schema", with refusals and token limits named as exceptions

problems: hint ('one of these changes what the model is allowed to emit; the others only ask for it more clearly') maps one-to-one onto the key's 'constrain the reply'
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs - "Structured outputs constrain Claude's responses to follow a specific schema"; output_config.format + strict:true; "beta headers are no longer required"
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs - "always generate responses that adhere to your supplied [JSON Schema]"; refusal and max-token truncation named as exceptions
verification.notes: Both vendor claims in the explanation verified, including that Anthropic's structured outputs are now GA with output_config.format and that refusals and truncation remain exceptions.

items.objective: Describe prompt injection: attacker text inside the model's input redirecting its behavior.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
correct option is markedly longer than the distractors
distractors (overheating the server, lowering the temperature remotely) are jokes rather than other attacks a learner might confuse this with
explanation restates the key
items.rationale: The highest-consequence concept in the level with a correct key, undermined by joke distractors and a length clue. Contrasting it with three other attacks makes the definition do work.
evidence: knowledge: OWASP lists prompt injection as the top LLM application risk; instructions and data share one token sequence with no trust boundary

problems: hint states the key's mechanism (attacker text landing inside the model's one token sequence), so the key is pickable without reading the options
evidence: knowledge: instructions, user text, retrieved documents and tool output share one token sequence with no trust boundary
knowledge: OWASP ranks prompt injection first among LLM application risks
verification.notes: Options and explanation are sound - flooding, key guessing and window overflow are real neighboring attacks - so only the hint is amended.

items.objective: Define reinforcement learning by its feedback signal: reward and penalty from an environment.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback with a tag echo
explanation describes the key only; it never contrasts the reward signal with labeled pairs, which is the misconception the options are built around
items.rationale: Correct and clearly written, with distractors that map onto the other paradigms; the hint is boilerplate and the explanation misses the contrast. Naming RLHF connects the paradigm to the models this audience actually calls.

items.objective: Know what a skip link gives a keyboard user on a page with repeated navigation.

https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/bypass-blocks.html : sufficient technique G1, "Adding a link at the top of each page that goes directly to the main content area"; without it users "might have to make dozens of keystrokes before reaching a link in the main content area"
verification.notes: Hint asks rather than asserts and the distractors are not competing; the hidden-until-focused detail in the explanation is accurate.

items.objective: Distinguish disabled (unfocusable, events blocked) from aria-disabled (state announced only).
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
items.rationale: Verified on both halves, and the explanation names the trade-off (the control stays reachable, but you must block the action yourself). Content sits above the level-2 band, which the topic's accessibility-throughout brief allows.
evidence: node: jsdom, click() on <button disabled> did not fire its listener (0 calls) while click() on <button aria-disabled="true"> did (1 call)

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-disabled : "aria-disabled does not change the focusability of such elements"; functionality must be suppressed manually

items.objective: Recognise details/summary as a built-in disclosure widget with toggle, keyboard support and announced state.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/details : the open attribute controls the state, Space toggles the widget when the summary is focused, the summary labels the widget and the open/closed state is exposed to assistive technology
node: jsdom 30.0.1, <details> with no open attribute reports open === false

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/details : "creates a disclosure widget in which information is visible only when the widget is toggled into an open state"; "When the user clicks on the widget or focuses it then presses the space bar, it 'twists' open"

verification.notes: Hint points at the reimplementation cost without asserting the answer; British "behaviour" in option 1 and the explanation is pre-existing, not introduced by this rewrite.

items.objective: Know what an associated label gives a control beyond a caption: an accessible name and a bigger hit target.
defects: the keyed option is markedly longer than three one-word distractors
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
items.rationale: Both halves of the key are documented and the explanation lands the placeholder contrast; the option lengths are the only real defect besides the hint.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/label : "That increased hit area for focusing the input provides an advantage to anyone trying to activate it - including those using a touch-screen device"; the label is programmatically associated with the control
verification.notes: Both halves of the key are documented; the hint points at the click behavior and leaves the accessible-name half to the learner.

items.objective: Associate a label with a control the way the browser actually reads: for pointing at id, or wrapping.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
items.rationale: The distractors are the three misconceptions learners actually hold, and the explanation adds the wrapping case without muddying the key. Only the hint fails.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/label : the for attribute must match the control's id (explicit association, recommended) or the control may be nested inside the label; class or adjacency is not an association

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/label : "There are two ways to associate a <label> with a form control", explicit (for matching the control's id) and implicit (nesting the control inside the label)
verification.notes: The explanation's wrapping aside matches the documented second form, and class or adjacency creates no association.

items.objective: Diagnose an empty submitted field: form data is serialised by name, so a control without one is not sent.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
items.rationale: Framed as a debugging symptom rather than a definition, which is what makes it worth keeping, and it is verified. Only the hint fails.
evidence: node: jsdom, new FormData(form) for a form holding <input name="a" value="1"> and <input id="b" value="2"> produced [["a","1"]] — the unnamed control is not serialised
node: jsdom 30.0.1, new FormData(form) over <input name="a" value="1">, <input id="b" value="2">, <input name="c" value="3"> produced [["a","1"],["c","3"]] - the id-only control is not serialized
verification.notes: Hint describes the role of the attribute without naming it, so the learner still has to know which one it is.

items.objective: Explain why a document has at most one main and what a second one costs a landmark user.
defects: distractor 3 ("It is required for the page to validate") is factually true: the spec forbids more than one non-hidden main, so a conformance checker does flag it
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation never says that browsers do render a second main, which is what makes distractor 0 tempting
items.rationale: The objective is sound but the fourth option is a true statement, so two options answer the question as asked. Replacing that distractor and naming the validation fact in the explanation fixes it.
evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html : "A document must not have more than one main element that does not have the hidden attribute specified."
https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/ : main -> role=main

cs.notes: "conformance checker" rendered as "validátor" — the Czech term developers use for the W3C checker; slightly narrower than the English.

evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html : "A document must not have more than one main element that does not have the hidden attribute specified."
https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/ : main -> role=main
verification.notes: The explanation's split between "nothing enforced at runtime" and "the spec does forbid it, so a conformance checker reports it" is exactly right, and the replacement SEO distractor is not defensible.

items.objective: Choose an input type for what it changes on a phone, and know the limits of its built-in check.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/input/email : "your site must not use this validation for any security purposes. You must verify the email address on the server side"

verification.notes: The reviewer's citation for the keyboard half is not on the page it names, but the claim holds and the other three options are false regardless.

items.objective: Understand required as a browser-side constraint plus an announced state, not a server guarantee.
defects: the keyed option is markedly longer and is the only two-part option, which flags it
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
items.rationale: Both claims in the key are documented and the explanation makes the security point without overstating it; the option lengths need levelling.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/required : "Assistive technology should inform the user that the form control is mandatory based on the required attribute"
verification.notes: The explanation keeps the client-side scope honest without claiming the attribute is a server-side guarantee, which is the trap in distractor 1.

items.objective: Know that a shared name makes radios one exclusive group, and that fieldset labels the group without creating it.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback

items.objective: Attach a validation message to its field programmatically so a screen-reader user hears it with the field.

items.objective: Write alt text that carries what the image contributes in the context where it appears.

items.objective: Set width and height so the browser can reserve space from the aspect ratio and avoid layout shift.

items.objective: Understand srcset as delegating the rendition choice to the browser, which knows the display and the network.

verification.notes: The expanded explanation is correct, including scoping sizes to width descriptors and attributing deferral to loading="lazy".

items.objective: Choose picture over srcset when the image itself changes, not only its size.

items.objective: Read heading levels as document structure rather than text size, and see what skipping a level claims.

verification.notes: Key and explanation are correct and the replacement distractors are both false, so only the hint needed loosening.

items.objective: Know what loading="lazy" defers, and where applying it hurts.

items.objective: Know what spoken video content owes users who cannot hear it: captions, and a transcript when it matters.

items.objective: Use figure with figcaption to express that a caption belongs to its content as one unit.

items.objective: Know that list markup conveys the item count and position, which repeated divs cannot.

items.objective: Choose ol when order carries meaning, judged by meaning rather than by wanting numbers.

items.objective: Express term-and-description pairs with dl, dt and dd rather than faking the pairing visually.
